facts.claim: Only 799 (0.04%) of the 1.9 million known recent species are recorded as extinct, which questions the reality of the crisis.
facts.quote: only 799 (0.04%) of the 1.9 million known recent species are recorded as extinct, questioning the reality of the crisis.

facts.claim: Extrapolation from a random sample of land snail species suggests we may already have lost 7% (130,000 extinctions) of the species on Earth.
facts.quote: we may already have lost 7% (130,000 extinctions) of the species on Earth.

facts.claim: In a sample of nearly half of known vertebrate species, 32% (8,851/27,600) are decreasing in population size and range.
facts.quote: In our sample, comprising nearly half of known vertebrate species, 32% (8,851/27,600) are decreasing; that is, they have decreased in population size and range.

facts.claim: In 177 mammals with detailed data, all have lost 30% or more of their geographic ranges and more than 40% of the species have experienced severe population declines.
facts.quote: In the 177 mammals for which we have detailed data, all have lost 30% or more of their geographic ranges and more than 40% of the species have experienced severe population declines (>80% range shrinkage).

facts.claim: If all now-endangered genera were to vanish by 2,100, extinction rates would be 354 (average) or 511 (for mammals) times higher than background rates.
facts.quote: If all now-endangered genera were to vanish by 2,100, extinction rates would be 354 (average) or 511 (for mammals) times higher than background rates

facts.claim: The average rate of vertebrate species loss over the last century is up to 100 times higher than the background rate.
facts.quote: the average rate of vertebrate species loss over the last century is up to 100 times higher than the background rate.

research.angle: While official records of extinction are low, data on vertebrate species and genera suggest current loss rates are significantly higher than background levels.
research.verdict: The evidence indicates that vertebrate species and genera are being lost at rates far exceeding natural background levels, though the total number of known extinctions remains low.
research.caveat: Many estimates of the extinction crisis are based on extrapolations or focus on vertebrates, potentially masking the status of invertebrates which represent the bulk of biodiversity.
